knowledge_fragments.content: Presentation: A 7-year-old male patient, initially treated at the age of 3 years for acute abdominal pain, was found to have a rectal polyp and hyperpigmented maculae on the lips and oral mucosa. His family history includes similar findings in his mother, who was identified with these features at the age of 25 years. Since the initial findings, the patient has not been consistently monitored due to various factors related to compliance and resource availability. Throughout this period, the patient has experienced chronic rectal bleeding.. Confirmed diagnosis: Peutz–Jeghers syndrome. Differential diagnosis includes: Peutz–Jeghers syndrome.
knowledge_fragments.title: Case report: Peutz–Jeghers syndrome

knowledge_fragments.content: MVT presentation can be acute, subacute, or chronic. Acute thrombosis is associated with a bowel infarction in one-third of the of patients, and the mortality rate of MVT is 20%. In the vast majority of patients, the onset of MVT is characterised by acute abdominal pain. Other common symptoms include diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, and lower gastrointestinal bleeding. MTV is associated with EHPVO in 65% of patients, and chronic presentation with no acute abdominal pain and extensive venous collateral circulation is common.

knowledge_fragments.content: Presentation: A 30-year-old female presented 2 months after sustaining trauma to the right ankle from a fall off a bike. Due to significant pain and swelling, she was treated conservatively and her ankle was immobilized in a below-knee splint for 8 weeks. She was instructed to avoid bearing weight on the affected limb throughout this period. Upon removal of the splint, she continued to experience severe pain and swelling and remained unable to bear weight.. Confirmed diagnosis: Complex Regional Pain Syndrome. Differential diagnosis includes: Complex Regional Pain Syndrome.
knowledge_fragments.title: Case report: Complex Regional Pain Syndrome

knowledge_fragments.content:
Chronic abdominal pain (CAP) persists for more than 3 mo either continuously or intermittently.

Intermittent pain may be referred to as recurrent abdominal pain (RAP).

Acute abdominal pain

is

discussed elsewhere. CAP occurs any time after 5 yr of age. Up to 10% of children require evaluation for

RAP. About 2% of adults, predominantly women, have CAP (a much higher percentage of adults have

some type of chronic GI symptoms, including nonulcer dyspepsia and various bowel disturbances).

Nearly all patients with CAP have had prior medical evaluation that did not yield a diagnosis after history,

physical, and basic testing.

knowledge_fragments.content: Presentation: A 7-year-old male patient, initially treated at the age of 3 years for acute abdominal pain, was found to have a rectal polyp and hyperpigmented maculae on the lips and oral mucosa. His family history includes similar findings in his mother, who was identified with these features at the age of 25 years. Since the initial findings, the patient has not been consistently monitored due to various factors related to compliance and resource availability. Throughout this period, the patient has experienced chronic rectal bleeding. The histopathological exam of the gastric poly and both recto-anal polyps did not reveal any signs of dysplasia, showing specific hamartomatous polyps.. Confirmed diagnosis: Peutz–Jeghers syndrome. Differential diagnosis includes: Peutz–Jeghers syndrome.

knowledge_fragments.content: Acute appendicitis (AA), which is one of the leading causes of lower abdominal pain, causes patients to go to the emergency department, and it is the most commonly diagnosed disease among young patients who are hospitalized with acute abdominal pain. Approximately 7%–10% of the general population experiences AA, with the highest incidence occurring in the second and third decades of life, and 7%–10% of all emergency department visits are due to acute abdominal pain. Different geographical areas are reported to have different infection risks. United States residents are reported to be at an 8% lifetime infection risk, while European and African residents are at a 2% lifetime infection risk. There are also differences among countries in per capita income, disease severity, and types of surgical management for affected patients.
knowledge_fragments.title: Economic Evaluation of Acute Appendicitis Therapeutic Interventions: A Systematic Review. > Introduction

knowledge_fragments.content: Presentation: A 58-year-old Caucasian female was admitted to the surgical department of our hospital for acute abdominal pain accompanied by vomiting. She had undergone a cholecystectomy 12 years prior. Physical examination showed tenderness upon palpation in the right epigastrium. Ultrasonography of the abdomen identified the presence of gallstones in the common bile duct. An endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography was performed to remove three gallstones.. Confirmed diagnosis: left venous renal entrapment syndrome. Differential diagnosis includes: left venous renal entrapment syndrome.
knowledge_fragments.title: Case report: left venous renal entrapment syndrome

knowledge_fragments.content: Postoperative bariatric patients require prompt imaging evaluation whenever complications are suspected, as early diagnosis is critical to reducing morbidity. Indications for imaging include any clinical signs of an anastomotic leak (such as unexplained tachycardia, fever, severe abdominal or chest pain, and oliguria) within the first days after surgery, signs of sepsis or peritonitis, or persistent postoperative ileus beyond the expected recovery period. In the early postoperative phase (generally within 10–14 days), a leak is one of the most feared complications and typically presents with acute abdominal pain, fever, tachycardia, and often hypotension. Any such presentation warrants immediate imaging to confirm a leak or identify intra-abdominal collections. Similarly, unexplained abdominal pain in later postoperative periods raises concern for internal hernia in RYGB patients or strictures causing obstruction in sleeve gastrectomy patients. For instance, months to years after RYGB, intermittent colicky pain, postprandial vomiting, or signs of small-bowel obstruction are red flags for an internal hernia through a mesenteric defect.
knowledge_fragments.title: Endoscopic Management of Post-Bariatric Surgery Complications: Diagnostic Work-Up and Innovative Approaches for Leak, Fistula, and Stricture Management. > 3. Radiological Assessment of Post-Bariatric Surgery Complications > 3.1. Indications for Imaging in Post-Bariatric Patients
